A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Puppeteer research and have readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends after its references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–D. Their absence from the supplied v1 is established, rather than an extraction gap.

before.justification: Table 1 reports original evaluations on GSM-Hard, MMLU-Pro, SRDD, and CommonGen-Hard. Figures 2–7 report learning dynamics, topology analyses, and sensitivity experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds cost and performance trajectories, agent-interaction examples, and an ALFWorld execution case study in Appendix A.

M1.justification: The centralized agent-selection procedure, REINFORCE optimization, aggregation, and quality–cost reward remain unchanged. Appendix B documents agent prompts; Appendix A.4 applies the framework to another environment without introducing a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: The four quantitative benchmarks are retained. Appendix A.4 adds ALFWorld embodied interaction, illustrated through one THOR task involving a remote control and floor lamp. This extends coverage to an interactive scenario, but no aggregate ALFWorld evaluation is reported.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same foundation-model comparators, Self-Refine, AFlow, MacNet, and EvoAgent in both model subspaces. The added embodied case study introduces no evaluated comparator; the new related-work citations are not additional baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 adds evaluation using performance divided by token cost. The new ALFWorld case uses a maximum chain length of 50, one exploration trajectory, and GPT-4o-mini for all agents. Existing benchmark settings are unchanged; the explicit 200-sample optimization limit is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: Appendix A substantially expands analysis of efficiency and collaboration: cost dynamics across the remaining model configurations, performance-per-token trajectories, concrete agent-interaction motifs, and an embodied execution case study. The original reward-weight and depth/width sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are supplied. LOWESS smoothing is retained for the additional curves; the computational-resource ranges are not reported as uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 is numerically unchanged, including the evolved Titan Puppeteer average of 0.7731. However, Figures 8–9 add extensive cost, agent-count, and performance/cost trajectories, including settings without consistent improvement. Figures 10–11 add qualitative interaction and embodied-execution evidence, substantially expanding the reported results.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 introduces the performance/cost score, explicitly defined as task performance divided by token cost. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition. The graph and Markov formulations, optimization objective, and reward equations (1)–(6) remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: dynamic centralized orchestration, reinforcement-driven adaptation, improved quality and efficiency, and emergent compact cyclic structures. The abstract's added code link does not alter these scientific claims.

C2.justification: Appendices A and C add explanations for uneven efficiency gains, possible limitations from optimization budget and hyperparameters, and difficulties comparing training costs across methods. Appendix D newly identifies coarse terminal rewards, a fixed agent/tool pool, miscoordination, and deceptive agreement as limitations. These substantially expand the qualifications surrounding the retained claims.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link, agent/action inventories, and role and action prompt templates in Appendix B. It explicitly documents the 200-sample optimization limit and reports eight A800 GPUs, 28.8–78.4 GB peak memory per GPU, and 2–6 hours of training in Table 3. These substantially improve implementation and resource disclosure.

R1.justification: Seven cited works are added, with the previous references retained. Section 4 now acknowledges classical multi-agent reinforcement learning as inspiration for coordination and role specialization; additional appendix citations include ALFWorld, AlphaMath, and MindStar. The principal positioning against LLM-based orchestration methods remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and nearly all existing prose are retained. v2 clarifies the explanation accompanying Equation (6), updates contact and conference information, adds an acknowledgement, and organizes new material into appendices. There is little rewriting or restructuring of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The appendix introduces extensive multi-panel plots, agent-topology diagrams, an environment-frame sequence, boxed prompt templates, and two tables. Figure 8 both redisplays the existing Titan curves and adds other configurations. Main-text figures are also repositioned or resized, notably Figures 2–3.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves evidential completeness and reproducibility: it supplies cost evidence referenced but absent from v1, documents agent prompts and computational requirements, and explains settings where efficiency gains are inconsistent. Its concrete limitations also make the retained claims easier to assess. The ALFWorld evidence remains illustrative and repeated-run uncertainty is still unreported, but these limits do not negate the substantial gains in documentation and empirical scrutiny.
